notes: Source-posture packet for the claim that the White House ballroom and other White House construction cost taxpayers $0. The packet preserves the difference between privately funded ballroom components, government-funded security work, the integrated East Wing/military-security complex, and the broader White House construction program.

sources.title: The White House Announces White House Ballroom Construction to Begin
supported_record: The White House stated that President Trump and other donors committed funds necessary to build an approximately $200 million ballroom structure.
The same announcement separately stated that the United States Secret Service would provide necessary security enhancements and modifications.
limitations: The statement establishes the administration's announced funding posture, not final audited project expenditures.
It does not establish that all integrated security, underground, demolition, infrastructure, maintenance-account, or related White House construction costs are privately funded.

sources.title: National Park Service, et al. v. National Trust for Historic Preservation — Application for Stay
supported_record: The federal government's Supreme Court filing characterizes the East Wing undertaking as an integrated military complex that includes a secure ballroom space.
This official characterization supports treating the ballroom and security construction as physically and operationally integrated for scope analysis.
limitations: The filing advocates the government's legal position and is not an independent accounting audit.
It does not by itself resolve the exact allocation of public versus private funds.

sources.title: National Park Service East Wing modernization and State Ballroom FONSI appendix
supported_record: The NPS environmental record describes a selected action for East Wing modernization and State Ballroom construction, including replacement of the existing East Wing with a new building housing the ballroom.
The official record treats the work as a modernization action on the White House grounds rather than only a detached event-space purchase.
limitations: Environmental review records do not provide a complete expenditure ledger.
Funding-source attribution still requires appropriations, transfer, obligation, contract, and donor records.

sources.title: Trump administration set to spend at least $900 million on White House construction, Washington Post reports
supported_record: Reuters reported at least $900 million in planned White House construction projects.
Reuters reported financing that included funds collected from government agencies as well as private donors and routed through a White House maintenance account.
limitations: Reuters is secondary to the underlying planning and financial records.
The underlying agency transfer, maintenance-account, obligation, and contract records remain required for primary-source reconstruction.

sources.title: Trump's ballroom costs are rising. What we know about the secret underground bunker
supported_record: Axios reported an approximately $600 million integrated East Wing ballroom and underground security project.
Axios reported that roughly half of that broader project cost was expected to be taxpayer funded.
limitations: The reported allocation must be reconciled against primary government accounting and contractor records.
The figure may reflect a different project scope than earlier $200 million, $250 million, or $400 million public estimates.

sources.title: Supreme Court lets Trump continue work on White House ballroom for now
supported_record: Reuters reported that the Supreme Court issued an administrative stay allowing construction to continue temporarily.
Reuters described the ballroom as part of a larger military and security complex.
limitations: The administrative stay is procedural and does not finally resolve legal authority or funding questions.
The article's $400 million characterization must be scope-reconciled against other estimates.
